items.name: iOS
items.why: Native and Flutter apps. They talk to the APIs with a device token, never a login screen.

items.name: Android
items.why: Same device-token model. Push arrives through Firebase; purchases arrive as Google Play notifications.

items.name: Web · React
items.why: A React 19 shell over the control-plane API. Public sites are server-rendered.
items.instead_of: Vue. Equivalent; the team already knew React.

name: Edge
tagline: before the request reaches the app

items.name: Cloudflare
items.why: DNS and proxy in front of everything. The client sees an edge address, never the origin. TLS ends close to the visitor.
items.instead_of: Route 53 alone. Rejected: no proxy, no edge TLS.

items.name: nginx
items.why: Takes the request from Cloudflare, adds forwarding headers and hands it to an Octane worker pool or PHP-FPM. Its request id becomes the trace id.
items.instead_of: Caddy. Fine, but the nginx configs are shared across the whole fleet.

items.name: CloudFront
items.why: Only where egress cost proved it: the two buckets behind most of the storage bill. Roughly a hundred dollars a month saved, with no app change.
items.instead_of: CloudFront everywhere. Rejected: most buckets do not move enough bytes.

items.name: Load balancer
items.why: One entry point, strict TLS end to end, and a place to move traffic between machines without a DNS change.
items.instead_of: Public IPs behind Cloudflare. That is today's setup, and it is being retired.

items.name: PHP · Laravel
items.why: One framework for every API and the control plane: one skeleton, one deploy script, two base images. The long tail of small apps stays cheap to keep alive.
items.instead_of: Node or Go per API. Rejected: a small team cannot carry two ecosystems for one job.

items.name: Octane · Swoole
items.why: The app boots once per worker, not once per request. Used only where traffic asks for it. Quiet apps stay on PHP-FPM, which has no long-lived state to leak.
items.instead_of: FrankenPHP or RoadRunner. Equivalent; Swoole was already proven here.

items.name: Node.js · Socket.IO
items.why: Long-lived connections for assistants, signalling and messaging, beside the PHP APIs. A process-per-request runtime is the wrong tool for a socket that stays open.
items.instead_of: Polling over HTTP. Rejected: latency and battery.

items.name: JWT · API tokens
items.why: Device JWTs for mobile clients, API tokens for the panels. Every request is attributable and revocable, and nobody sees a login form.
items.instead_of: A full OAuth server. Rejected: flows the apps do not need.

items.name: libvips · ffmpeg
items.why: Images are resized and optimised on write through libvips. Video goes through ffmpeg in a worker. Nothing heavy runs inside a request.
items.instead_of: GD and Imagick. Slower and hungrier at the sizes involved.

items.name: OpenAI · Gemini
items.why: Text and vision, behind queued workers. Every provider call is wrapped, so a swap is a config change and one class, not a rewrite.
items.instead_of: One provider for everything. Rejected: quality and price differ per task.

items.name: Replicate · fal
items.why: Hosted models for image and video generation. Where a provider was too slow or too expensive, the same models run self-hosted on RunPod.

items.name: ElevenLabs
items.why: Text to speech for the voice products. Audio is chunked and streamed to storage before the device is notified.

items.name: App Store · Google Play
items.why: Server notifications and receipt validation on both stores, handled synchronously and turned into 17 typed subscription events by one shared package.
items.instead_of: Trusting the client. Never.

items.name: Adapty
items.why: Paywalls and experiments without building them. Its webhooks are queued and handled async, next to the native store notifications, so a renewal missed by one source is caught by the other.
items.instead_of: RevenueCat. Equivalent; Adapty was already in the apps.

items.name: Firebase FCM
items.why: One notification package with a driver switch. The move off the old provider did not touch a single notification class.
items.instead_of: Staying on the old provider. Rejected on cost and lock-in.

items.name: MySQL 8
items.why: One database per app keeps the blast radius small and lets the control plane attach to each. Self-hosted on EC2 today for cost; a managed multi-AZ setup is the next step once data is separated from compute.
items.instead_of: PostgreSQL. Fine; MySQL is what the fleet already runs.

items.name: Redis
items.why: One shared instance on the data server, so app servers can be replaced without touching state. Rate limits, cache and the hot apps' queues live here.
items.instead_of: Memcached. Rejected: no persistence, no queues.

items.name: ClickHouse
items.why: A read-only mirror built for aggregates. Dashboard queries went from thirty seconds on MySQL to well under one.
items.instead_of: MySQL read replicas. Rejected: same engine, same slow aggregates.

items.name: PeerDB
items.why: Streams MySQL binlogs into ClickHouse, seconds behind, so production never runs an analytics query.
items.instead_of: Nightly dumps. Rejected: a day stale and heavy on the source.

items.name: MinIO
items.why: S3-compatible object storage on the data server. The landing zone between PeerDB and ClickHouse.

items.name: S3
items.why: Every upload and every generated asset. Public reads go through CloudFront where the bill asked for it.

items.name: AWS EC2 · Graviton
items.why: ARM instances by default: cheaper for the same work. Sizes come from thirty-day graphs, not habit.
items.instead_of: x86. Kept only where a dependency demands it; so far none has.

items.name: ECS · ECR
items.why: The container pilot. A task has a memory limit, so an out-of-memory kills one task and not its neighbours. An image is an immutable deploy.
items.instead_of: Fargate. Rejected at this profile: a 20 to 60 percent premium over the EC2 launch type.

items.name: Docker
items.why: Two base images cover the fleet: PHP-FPM and Octane. Dependencies are installed at build time, so private packages need no credentials at runtime.

items.name: GitLab CI · Envoy
items.why: Release folders and a current symlink, shared .env and storage, manual production jobs from main. Every app deploys the same way, from inside the network. The container pilot ships an image instead.
items.instead_of: GitHub Actions. Rejected: repos, runners and secrets stay inside.

items.name: Supervisor · PM2
items.why: Supervisor keeps queue workers and schedulers alive for PHP; PM2 does the same for the Node socket services.
items.instead_of: systemd units per app. More ceremony for the same result.

items.name: WireGuard
items.why: An API leases peers across a fleet of nodes and enforces those leases against payment events on a schedule.
items.instead_of: OpenVPN. Rejected: heavier, slower to provision.

items.name: Nightwatch
items.why: Exceptions, slow routes, slow jobs and scheduled tasks, per app. It is how the silent failure in the push package was found.

items.name: Sentry
items.why: Kept where it already was. Nightwatch covers new work.

items.name: Telescope
items.why: Local debugging only. Left on by default it records every scheduled task run, so every production .env pins it off.

items.name: Zabbix
items.why: CPU, memory and disk on every EC2, with alerts to Slack. The graphs that decide instance sizes come from here.
items.instead_of: CloudWatch alarms, which are not set up yet. On the list.

items.name: Slack alerts
items.why: Apps post their own alerts: failed jobs, provider errors, unusual purchase events.

items.name: Telegram
items.why: A second channel, for the alerts that must wake someone up.
